exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Direction Vector of a Line Given as the Intersection of Two Planes

question.text: Find a direction vector of the line that is given as the intersection of the following two planes: \[ \begin{cases} -x+z-3 = 0 \\ 3x+2y-5 = 0 \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
First, we notice:

  • For the plane $-x+z-3 = 0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle -1,0,1 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $3x+2y-5 = 0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 3,2,0 \rangle.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{v} &= \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 \\[5pt] & = \langle -1, 0, 1 \rangle \times \langle 3, 2, 0 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 0 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=-2\mathbf{i} +3 \mathbf{j} -2\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle -2, 3, -2 \rangle \end{align*}

question.text: Find a direction vector of the line that is given as the intersection of the following two planes: \[ \begin{cases} 5x-4y = 0 \\ 4y-5z= 0 \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
First, we notice:

  • For the plane $5x-4y = 0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 5,-4,0 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $4y-5z= 0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 0,4,-5 \rangle.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{v} &= \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 \\[5pt] & = \langle 5,-4,0 \rangle \times \langle 0,4,-5 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 5 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -5 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=20\mathbf{i} +25 \mathbf{j} + 20\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle 20, 25, 20 \rangle \end{align*}

  • For the plane $2y-3z-25 = 0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 0,2,-3 \rangle.$

question.text: Find a direction vector of the line that is given as the intersection of the following two planes: \[ \begin{cases} x+2y-5 = 0 \\ 2x-y+z+1 = 0 \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
First, we notice:

  • For the plane $x+2y-5 = 0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 1,2,0 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $2x-y+z+1 = 0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 2,-1,1 \rangle.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{v} &= \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 \\[5pt] & = \langle 1, 2, 0 \rangle \times \langle 2, -1, 1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} -5\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle 2, -1, -5 \rangle \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Given as the Intersection of Two Planes

question.text:
The intersection of the planes $3x+6y+3z=0$ and $x-y+2z+3=0$ is given by the line

\[ \mathbf r(t) = \langle a_1,a_2 ,0\rangle + t \mathbf b, \quad t\in(-\infty,\infty). \]

Calculate $a_1+a_2,$ and find a possible direction vector $\mathbf b.$
question.explanation:
We're given that there exists a point on the line where $z=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation gives

\[ 3x+6y+3(0)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=-2y, \]

and substituting $z=0$ and $x=-2y$ into the second equation gives

\begin{align*} x-y+2z+3 &=0\\[3pt] -2y-y+2(0)+3&=0 \\[3pt] -3y &=-3 \\[3pt] y &= 1. \end{align*}

Therefore, $x=-2y=-2$ and $\mathbf a = \langle -2,1,0\rangle$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

  • For the plane $3x+6y+3z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 3,6,3 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $x-y+2z+3=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 1,-1,2 \rangle.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle 3,6,3 \rangle \times \langle 1,-1,2 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=15\mathbf{i} -3\mathbf{j} -9\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle 15, -3, -9 \rangle \end{align*}

We can pick any vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2$ as a direction vector of the line. So, let \[ \mathbf{b} = \dfrac{1}{3} (\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2) = \langle 5, -1, -3 \rangle. \]

The equation of the line is:

\begin{align*} \mathbf r(t) &= \mathbf a + t\mathbf b\\[5pt] \mathbf r(t) &= \langle -2,1,0\rangle + t\langle 5, -1, -3\rangle\\[5pt] \end{align*}

Finally then, $a_1 + a_2 = -2+1 = -1,$ and $\mathbf b = \langle 5, -1, -3\rangle.$

example.title: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Given as the Intersection of Two Planes

question.text:
The intersection of the planes $-x+z-1=0$ and $y+z+5=0$ is given by the line

\[ \mathbf r(t) = \langle a_1, a_2, 0\rangle + t \mathbf b, \quad t\in(-\infty,\infty). \]

Calculate $a_1+a_2,$ and find a possible direction vector $\mathbf b.$
question.explanation:
We're given that there exists a point on the line where $z=0.$ Substituting this to the first equation gives

\[ -x+0-1=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=-1, \]

and substituting $z=0$ into the second equation gives

\[ y+0+5=0\qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad y=-5. \]

Therefore, $\mathbf a = \langle -1,-5,0\rangle$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

  • For the plane $-x+z-1=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle -1,0,1 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $y+z+5=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 0,1,1 \rangle.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{b} &= \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 \\[5pt] & = \langle-1,0,1 \rangle \times \langle 0,1,1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=-\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} -\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle -1, 1, -1 \rangle \end{align*}

Thus, the equation of the line is:

\begin{align*} \mathbf r(t) &= \mathbf a + t\mathbf b\\[5pt] \mathbf r(t) &= \langle -1,-5,0\rangle + t\langle -1, 1, -1\rangle\\[5pt] \end{align*}

Finally then, $a_1 + a_2 = -1+ (-5) = -6,$ and $\mathbf b = \langle -1,1,-1\rangle.$

example.title: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Given as the Intersection of Two Planes

question.text:
The intersection of the planes $-x+y-2z=0$ and $-x-2y+z-3=0$ is given by the line

\[ \mathbf r(t) = \langle a_1,a_2,0 \rangle + t \mathbf b, \quad t\in(-\infty,\infty). \]

Calculate $a_1+a_2,$ and find a possible direction vector $\mathbf b.$
question.explanation:
We're given that there exists a point on the line where $z=0.$ Substituting this to the first equation gives

\[ -x+y-2(0)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=y, \]

and substituting $z=0$ and $x=y$ into the second equation gives

\begin{align*} -x-2y+z-3 &= 0 \\[3pt] -y-2y+0-3 &= 0 \\[3pt] -3y &=3 \\[3pt] y &= -1. \end{align*}

Therefore, $x=y=-1$ and $\mathbf a = \langle -1,-1,0\rangle$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

  • For the plane $-x+y-2z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle -1,1,-2 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $-x-2y+z-3=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle -1,-2,1 \rangle.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle -1, 1, -2 \rangle \times \langle -1, -2, 1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=-3\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} +3\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle -3, 3, 3 \rangle \end{align*}

We can pick any vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2$ as a direction vector of the line. So, let \[ \mathbf{b} = \dfrac{1}{3} (\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2) = \langle -1, 1, 1 \rangle. \]

The equation of the line is:

\begin{align*} \mathbf r(t) &= \mathbf a + t\mathbf b\\[5pt] \mathbf r(t) &= \langle -1,-1,0\rangle + t\langle -1,1,1\rangle\\[5pt] \end{align*}

Finally then, $a_1 + a_2 = -1-1 = -2,$ and $\mathbf b = \langle -1,1,1\rangle.$

example.title: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Given as the Intersection of Two Planes

question.text:
The intersection of the planes $x+2y-4z+6=0$ and $x-4y+2z=0$ is given by the line

\[ \mathbf r(t) = \langle 0, a_2, a_3\rangle + t \mathbf b, \quad t\in(-\infty,\infty). \]

Calculate $a_2+a_3,$ and find a possible direction vector $\mathbf b.$
question.explanation:
We're given that there exists a point on the line where $x=0.$ Substituting this into the second equation gives

\[ 0-4y+2z=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad z=2y, \]

and substituting $x=0$ and $z=2y$ into the first equation gives

\begin{align*} x+2y-4z+6 &=0\\[3pt] 0+2y-4(2y)+6&=0 \\[3pt] -6y &=-6 \\[3pt] y &= 1. \end{align*}

Therefore, $z=2y=2$ and $\mathbf a = \langle 0,1,2\rangle$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

  • For the plane $x+2y-4z+6=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 1,2,-4 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $x-4y+2z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 1,-4,2 \rangle.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle1,2,-4 \rangle \times \langle 1,-4,2 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & 2 & -4 \\ 1 & -4 & 2 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=-12\mathbf{i} -6 \mathbf{j} -6\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle -12, -6, -6 \rangle \end{align*}

We can pick any vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2$ as a direction vector of the line. So, let \[\mathbf{b} =-\dfrac{1}{6}(\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2) = \langle 2, 1, 1 \rangle.\]

Hence, the equation of the line is:

\begin{align*} \mathbf r(t) &= \mathbf a + t\mathbf b\\[5pt] \mathbf r(t) &= \langle 0,1,2\rangle + t\langle 2, 1, 1\rangle\\[5pt] \end{align*}

Finally then, $a_2 +a_3 = 1+2 = 3,$ and $\mathbf b = \langle 2,1,1\rangle.$

example.title: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Given as the Intersection of Two Planes

question.text:
The intersection of the planes $x+2y+2z=0$ and $4x-2y+4z+8=0$ is given by the line

\[ \mathbf r(t) = \langle a_1,0 ,a_3\rangle + t \mathbf b, \quad t\in(-\infty,\infty). \]

Calculate $a_1+a_3,$ and find a possible direction vector $\mathbf b.$
question.explanation:
We're given that there exists a point on the line where $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation gives

\[ x+2(0)+2z=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=-2z, \]

and substituting $y=0$ and $x=-2z$ into the second equation gives

\begin{align*} 4x-2y+4z+8 &=0\\[3pt] 4(-2z)-2(0)+4z+8&=0 \\[3pt] -4z &=-8 \\[3pt] z &= 2. \end{align*}

Therefore, $x=-2z=-4$ and $\mathbf a = \langle -4,0,2\rangle$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

  • For the plane $x+2y+2z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 1,2,2 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $4x-2y+4z+8=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 4,-2,4 \rangle.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle 1,2,2 \rangle \times \langle 4,-2,4 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 4 & -2 & 4 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=12\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} -10\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle 12, 4, -10 \rangle \end{align*}

We can pick any vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2$ as a direction vector of the line. So, let \[ \mathbf{b} = \dfrac{1}{2} (\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2) = \langle 6, 2, -5 \rangle. \]

The equation of the line is:

\begin{align*} \mathbf r(t) &= \mathbf a + t\mathbf b\\[5pt] \mathbf r(t) &= \langle -4,0,2\rangle + t\langle 6, 2, -5\rangle\\[5pt] \end{align*}

Finally then, $a_1 + a_3 = -4+2 = -2,$ and $\mathbf b = \langle 6, 2, -5\rangle.$

exampleAnswers.title: Identifying the Intersection of Two Planes

question.text:
Given the two planes $3x+y-2z=0$ and $2x+y+3z+7=0$, which of the following statements are true?

  1. The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $\langle 5,-13,1 \rangle.$
  2. The planes are parallel.
  3. The planes intersect on a line.
question.explanation:
First, notice that:

  • For the plane $3x+y-2z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 3,1,-2 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $2x+y+3z+7=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 2,1,3 \rangle.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

  • Statement I is true. Computing the cross product of the normal vectors, we get \begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle 3, 1,-2 \rangle \times \langle 2, 1, 3 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 3 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=5\mathbf{i} - 13\mathbf{j} +\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle 5, -13, 1 \rangle \end{align*}

  • Statement II is false. Since $\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 \neq \mathbf{0}$, the vectors $\mathbf{n}_1$ and $\mathbf{n}_2$ are not parallel. As a result, the corresponding planes are not parallel either.

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, two non-parallel planes in $3$-dimensional space must intersect on a line.

Therefore, only I and III only are true.

question.text:
Given the two planes $3x-6y+1=0$ and $-x+2y=0$, which of the following statements are true?

  1. The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $ \mathbf{0}.$
  2. The planes are parallel but not coincident.
  3. The planes intersect in a straight line.
question.explanation:
First, notice that:

  • For the plane $3x-6y+1=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 3,-6,0 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $-x+2y=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle -1,2,0 \rangle.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, computing the cross product of the normal vectors, we get \begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & =\langle 3,-6,0 \rangle \times \langle -1,2,0 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 3 & -6 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 0 \end{array} \\[5pt] &= 0 \mathbf{i} + 0 \mathbf{j} + 0 \mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &=\mathbf{0}. \end{align*}

  • Statement II is true. Since $\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 =\mathbf{0}$, the vectors $\mathbf{n}_1$ and $\mathbf{n}_2$ are parallel. However, the second plane passes through the origin $O(0,0,0)$ but the first plane doesn't: \[3(0)-6(0)+1=1 \neq 0\] So, the planes are parallel but not coincident.

  • Statement III is false. Since planes are parallel but not coincident, they cannot intersect.

Therefore, only statements I and II are true.

question.text:
Given the two planes $x-2y+z=0$ and $x-y+1=0$, which of the following statements are true?

  1. The normal vectors of the planes are parallel.
  2. The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $\mathbf 0.$
  3. The planes intersect on a line.
question.explanation:
First, notice that:

  • For the plane $x-2y+z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 1,-2,1 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $x-y+1=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 1,-1,0 \rangle.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

  • Statements I and II are false. Indeed, computing the cross product of the normal vectors, we get \begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle 1,-2,1 \rangle \times \langle 1,-1,0 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} +\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle \neq \mathbf{0}. \end{align*} Since $\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 \neq \mathbf{0}$, the vectors $\mathbf{n}_1$ and $\mathbf{n}_2$ are not parallel.

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, two non-parallel planes in $3$-dimensional space must intersect on a line.

Therefore, only statement III is true.

question.text:
Given the two planes $x-3y+z=0$ and $2x-y+1=0$, which of the following statements are true?

  1. The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $ \langle 1, 5, 2 \rangle.$
  2. The planes intersect on a line.
  3. The planes are coincident.
question.explanation:
First, notice that:

  • For the plane $x-3y+z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 1,-3,1 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $2x-y+1=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 2,-1,0 \rangle.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

  • Statement I is false. Indeed, computing the cross product of the normal vectors, we get \begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle 1, -3, 1 \rangle \times \langle 2, -1, 0 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} +5\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle 1, 2, 5 \rangle \neq \langle 1, 5, 2 \rangle. \end{align*}

  • Statement II is true. Since $\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 \neq \mathbf{0}$, the vectors $\mathbf{n}_1$ and $\mathbf{n}_2$ are not parallel. Hence, the planes must intersect on a line.

  • Statement III is false. Indeed, two non-parallel planes cannot be coincident.

Therefore, only statement II is true.
